summary: The organization knows which laws and rules apply to its AI systems and records how it handles them.
Expectations for trustworthy AI are built into the organization's policies and day-to-day procedures.
The organization sets how much risk management each AI system needs, based on the risk it is willing to accept.
Transparent policies and controls define the risk management process and its results, in line with the organization's risk priorities.
The organization plans ongoing checks of its risk management, names who is responsible, and sets how often reviews happen.
The organization keeps a list of its AI systems and staffs that work according to its risk priorities.
There is a safe way to retire AI systems without creating new risks or making the organization less trustworthy.
Roles, responsibilities, and communication paths for AI risk work are written down and clear across the organization.
Staff and partners are trained so they can carry out AI risk duties in line with policies and agreements.
Senior leaders take responsibility for decisions about risks from developing and deploying AI systems.
Decisions about AI risk across the system lifecycle draw on people with a range of backgrounds, skills, and experience.
Policies define who does what when people and AI systems work together, including who oversees the system.
Policies encourage critical thinking and a safety-first approach so AI is designed and used in ways that limit harm.
Teams record the risks and impacts of the AI they design, deploy, and use, and they communicate those impacts more widely.
The organization has practices for testing AI, finding incidents, and sharing information about them.
The organization gathers and uses feedback from people outside the build team about how AI could affect individuals and society.
Reviewed feedback from relevant people is regularly built into how AI systems are designed and put into practice.
Policies address AI risks that come from third parties, including the risk of infringing someone else's intellectual property or other rights.
Backup plans exist for failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems that are treated as high risk.
The system's purpose, expected users, legal and social setting, and likely benefits and harms are understood and written down.
People from different disciplines and backgrounds help establish the context, and their participation is recorded.
The organization's mission and its goals for the AI technology are understood and documented.
The business reason for using the AI is clearly defined, or checked again for a system already in use.
The organization writes down how much AI risk it is willing to accept.
Relevant people agree on system requirements, such as respecting user privacy, and design choices account for social as well as technical effects.
The task the AI system will support, and the method used to carry it out, are defined.
The organization documents what the system does not know and how people are expected to use and oversee its results.
Needs for scientific integrity and for testing are identified, including how data are chosen and whether the system measures what it claims to measure.
The expected benefits of what the AI system is meant to do, and how well it should perform, are examined and documented.
The costs of AI errors and of how the system behaves, including costs that are not money, are examined against the organization's risk tolerance and documented.
The organization writes down where the system is meant to be applied, based on what it can do and the context it was built for.
The organization defines and checks how operators stay proficient with system performance, trustworthiness, and relevant standards.
Human oversight is defined, checked, and documented in line with the organization's governance policies.
The organization maps technical and legal risks in AI components, including third-party data or software and possible infringement of others' rights.
Internal risk controls for system components, including third-party AI technologies, are identified and documented.
For each impact, the organization estimates how likely it is and how large it could be, using expected use, similar past uses, public incidents, and outside feedback.
People and practices are in place to keep engaging relevant parties and to use their feedback on expected and unexpected impacts.
The organization chooses how to measure the AI risks found during mapping, starts with the most important ones, and records risks it will not or cannot measure.
Metrics and existing controls are reviewed regularly and updated, including when errors affect communities.
People who did not build the system, and outside experts or affected communities when the risk calls for it, take part in regular assessments.
Test sets, metrics, and the tools used to test, evaluate, validate, and verify the system are documented.
Tests that involve people follow human-subject protections and represent the population that matters.
Performance is measured in conditions similar to real deployment, and those measures are documented.
The behavior of the AI system and its parts is monitored while the system is in production.
The system is shown to be valid and reliable for deployment, and limits on using it outside the conditions it was built for are documented.
Safety risks are evaluated regularly, leftover risk stays within tolerance, and the system can fail safely if pushed beyond what it knows.
The system's security and ability to withstand disruption are evaluated and documented.
Risks related to transparency and accountability are examined and documented.
The model is explained, checked, and documented, and its outputs are interpreted in context so people can use and oversee it responsibly.
Privacy risks of the AI system are examined and documented.
Fairness and bias are evaluated, and the results are documented.
The environmental impact of training and managing the AI model is assessed and documented.
The organization checks whether its testing metrics and processes work, and documents that check.
The organization regularly finds and tracks known, unexpected, and newly emerging risks based on how the system actually performs in use.
The organization plans how to track risks that current measurement methods cannot assess well.
End users and affected communities can report problems and appeal outcomes, and that feedback is built into evaluation.
Ways of measuring AI risk are tied to the deployment setting and shaped by advice from domain experts and users.
Experts and other relevant people review measurement results to confirm the system still behaves as intended where it is deployed.
Measurable gains or drops in performance, drawn from affected communities and field data, are identified and documented.
The organization decides whether the AI system meets its purpose and whether development or deployment should go ahead.
Documented AI risks are ranked for action by impact, likelihood, and the resources or methods available.
Responses to the highest-priority risks are planned and documented, including whether to reduce, transfer, avoid, or accept each risk.
Risks that remain after treatment are documented for later acquirers of the system and for end users.
The resources needed to manage AI risk are considered, along with non-AI alternatives that could reduce the chance or size of harm.
Deployed AI systems are monitored so drift does not erode their value or pull them out of line with the context of use.
The organization follows a procedure to respond and recover when a risk it had not identified before appears.
Someone is assigned, and a mechanism is in place, to override or shut off systems that no longer behave as intended.
Risks and benefits from third-party resources are monitored regularly, and controls are applied and documented.
Pre-trained models used in development are included in regular monitoring and maintenance.
After deployment, the organization monitors the system, including user input, appeals, overrides, incidents, recovery, changes, and retirement.
System updates include measurable improvement work and regular contact with interested parties.
Incidents and errors are reported to relevant people, including affected communities, and tracking, response, and recovery steps are followed and documented.
